column1: login-timing|H|H4|authn|Login returns identical text, but nonexistent users respond much faster. Which weakness remains?|Account enumeration through timing|Session fixation through cookies|SQL injection through response headers|Cross-site request forgery through forms|Generic messages can still disclose account existence through repeatable timing differences. Compare controlled samples and investigate the different paths.|Equal text does not mean equal observable behavior.

reauth-change|H|H4|authn|A stolen active session can change the account's password without any further check. Which control best limits this action?|Reauthentication for sensitive changes|A longer public username|A new CSS theme for the form|Hiding the password-change menu|A fresh authentication check reduces reliance on possession of an existing session for high-impact changes.|A hidden menu does not protect its endpoint.

factor-types|H|H4|authn|A login asks for a password and a second memorized PIN. What does this establish?|Two knowledge secrets|Two independent factor categories|A possession and an inherence factor|Phishing-resistant authentication|Both answers are knowledge factors. Two steps do not necessarily provide two factor categories.|Count factor categories, not screens.

mfa-recovery|H|H4|authn|A hardware-key login can be bypassed through a password-only recovery endpoint. Where is the main weakness?|The weaker alternate authentication path|The key's asymmetric signature algorithm|The browser's preferred color scheme|The length of the recovery page URL|Recovery must provide assurance appropriate to the account. Strong primary authentication loses value when a weaker path replaces it.|Assess every path to the same account.

spray-control|H|H4|authn|Many accounts each receive one bad password attempt from the same source. Why may per-account lockout miss this?|Attempts are distributed across accounts|Each account exceeds its own threshold|Lockout cannot count failed attempts|TLS conceals attempts from the server|Password spraying deliberately stays below individual-account thresholds. Detection should consider source and aggregate patterns too.|A narrow counter can miss a broad campaign.

reset-single-use|H|H4|reset|A reset token still works after it successfully changes a password. What property is missing?|Single-use invalidation|URL percent encoding|A public certificate subject|A client-side password meter|Reset tokens should become invalid after successful use. Expiry and randomness address other token properties.|Short expiry does not make a token single-use.

reset-host|H|H4|reset|A reset link is built from an untrusted Host header. What is the relevant failure mode?|Reset links can point to an attacker-chosen host|Passwords become reversible hashes|Every cookie changes to HttpOnly|The database changes its isolation level|A trusted configured origin or validated host allowlist prevents request metadata from controlling sensitive links.|Request headers are not authoritative site configuration.

reset-enumeration|H|H4|reset|Reset says 'email sent' for members and 'unknown user' otherwise. What is disclosed?|Whether an account exists|Its password plaintext|Its session encryption key|Its exact database row count|Consistent messages and appropriate response timing reduce enumeration without exposing whether a user is registered.|A useful user experience must not disclose unnecessary account state.

reset-binding|H|H4|reset|A valid token for Alice can reset Bob by changing a separate username field. What should validation bind?|The token to its intended account|The token to the CSS stylesheet|The username to the User-Agent brand|The password to the page title|The server should derive the account from validated token state or securely enforce the association.|Possession of a valid token is not authority over every account.

logout-server|H|H11|session|Logout removes the browser cookie, but a copied cookie remains accepted. Which control failed?|Server-side session invalidation|Browser viewport detection|HTML entity encoding|Password complexity enforcement|The server must invalidate the session or otherwise reject it after logout. Deleting one browser's copy is insufficient.|Client cleanup and server revocation are separate.

rotation-login|H|H11|session|An anonymous session identifier remains unchanged after login. Which attack does rotation help prevent?|Session fixation|DNS zone transfer|SMTP open relay|SQL deadlock|An attacker who arranged the pre-login identifier may reuse the authenticated session. Rotate identifiers when authentication state changes.|Randomness alone does not address a previously known identifier.

idle-absolute|H|H11|session|An active session never expires while requests continue. Which limit caps its total lifetime?|Absolute timeout|Idle timeout only|Cookie path matching only|Login error text normalization|An absolute timeout applies regardless of recent activity. Idle timeout measures inactivity.|Continual activity can prevent an idle timeout indefinitely.

secure-httponly|H|H11|cookies|Which cookie attribute directly prevents ordinary document.cookie access to that cookie?|HttpOnly|Secure|Path|Expires|HttpOnly restricts script access. Secure restricts transport; neither stops a browser from making authenticated requests.|HttpOnly does not neutralize all consequences of XSS.

secure-transport|H|H11|cookies|A session cookie is HttpOnly but sent over HTTP. Which attribute addresses this transport issue?|Secure|Domain|Max-Age|SameSite|Secure limits sending the cookie to secure channels. HTTPS deployment and redirects still need appropriate configuration.|Script access and network transport are different protections.

domain-cookie|H|H11|cookies|Why can Domain=example.test broaden a session cookie's exposure compared with a host-only cookie?|It includes matching subdomains|It encrypts values for sibling hosts|It binds the cookie to one TCP port|It rejects every cross-site request|A Domain attribute extends scope to matching subdomains, potentially involving less trusted hosts.|Cookie scope follows host rules, not application ownership assumptions.

path-cookie|H|H11|cookies|Can Path=/admin be relied on as an authorization boundary between applications on one origin?|No; it mainly controls cookie attachment by path|Yes; it creates a separate browser origin|Yes; it makes the value cryptographically signed|No; it disables all cookies on the host|RFC 6265 cautions that cookie paths are not a reliable security boundary. Enforce authorization on the server.|Routing scope does not create a trust boundary.

url-session|H|H11|session|A session ID is carried in URL query strings. Which exposure is especially relevant?|Logs, history, and copied links may retain it|It always gains 256 bits of entropy|It automatically receives HttpOnly protection|It cannot be replayed after copying|URLs commonly pass through storage and sharing surfaces. Avoid carrying session secrets in URLs.|TLS does not remove URL retention at endpoints.

role-revoke|H|H11|authz|An administrator removes a user's role, but existing sessions retain that role for days. What needs review?|Authorization state refresh and revocation|The login page's font size|Only the user's password length|Only the certificate's serial number|Privilege removal must reach enforcement decisions within an acceptable interval. Stale cached claims can preserve removed access.|A correct role change can still have delayed security effect.

cache-session|H|H11|session|A shared proxy caches authenticated profile pages without varying by identity. What is at risk?|One user receiving another user's page|All passwords being rehashed with salts|Only browser-local session storage capacity|Only the HTTP request method's spelling|Sensitive authenticated responses need appropriate cache controls and cache-key design.|Authentication at the origin does not make every intermediary cache safe.

csrf-side-effect|H|H11|csrf|A GET endpoint changes a shipping address using the session cookie. Why is this risky?|Cross-site navigation can trigger a state change|GET cannot carry a query string|Browsers never attach cookies to navigation|TLS forbids state-changing GET requests|State changes should use appropriate methods and CSRF defenses. Do not assume an endpoint is safe merely because it uses GET.|Method choice and request-forgery protection both matter.

csrf-cors|H|H11|csrf|A site blocks reading cross-origin responses through CORS. Does that alone prevent CSRF?|No; some cross-origin requests can still be sent|Yes; it blocks all cross-origin network traffic|Yes; it invalidates all session cookies|No; because every CORS response is public|A forged request may cause a side effect without its response being readable. Apply CSRF defenses to state-changing cookie-authenticated actions.|Read permission differs from request transmission.

csrf-token-bind|H|H11|csrf|An attacker obtains a token from their own session and uses it with a victim's session successfully. What is missing?|Appropriate token binding or equivalent verification|A larger submit button|A predictable token prefix|A different response content type|A token should not authorize arbitrary other sessions. The defense must validate token authenticity and its required association.|Checking only that a token has the right format is insufficient.

csrf-subdomain|H|H11|csrf|Why can SameSite cookies leave risk from a compromised sibling subdomain?|Same-site is broader than same-origin|SameSite applies only to plaintext cookies|All subdomains share DOM access by default|SameSite removes server authorization checks|Site and origin are different concepts. A sibling host may be same-site while remaining a different origin.|Do not treat site membership as full trust.

csrf-json|H|H11|csrf|An API expects JSON but also accepts a simple form encoding without CSRF checks. What should be investigated?|Whether a cross-site form can reach the state change|Whether JSON is encrypted at rest|Whether all responses have equal length|Whether every request uses a fixed source port|Alternative accepted encodings can bypass assumptions about required preflight or custom headers.|Validate actual accepted request formats.

object-owner|H|H5|authz|A user changes /orders/41 to /orders/42 and sees another customer's receipt. Which check is missing?|Object-level authorization|Password hashing|DNSSEC validation|JavaScript minification|The server must enforce that the requester can access the specific order, irrespective of identifier predictability.|Unpredictable identifiers are useful but do not replace access checks.

function-role|H|H5|authz|A normal user cannot see Admin in the menu, but POST /admin/disable-user succeeds. What failed?|Function-level authorization|Login password verification|Browser cookie parsing|Certificate chain building|Authorization must protect the operation itself. Removing a navigation element is a presentation choice.|Test endpoints directly within the authorized assessment scope.

tenant-field|H|H5|authz|A request's tenantId is editable and determines the tenant queried, without comparison to the session. What is needed?|A trusted tenant authorization decision|A longer decimal tenant ID|Only a client-side disabled field|Only a lowercase JSON property name|The server must verify membership or derive the authorized tenant from trusted state. Client fields are untrusted.|Authentication does not establish every tenant context.

mass-assignment|H|H5|authz|A profile update copies every submitted field into the model, including isAdmin. What is the best correction?|Allowlist fields permitted for this operation|Require the field name to be uppercase|Hide isAdmin in the frontend schema|Accept it only through JSON POST|Restrict bindable fields and separately enforce permissions for privileged changes.|The input format does not establish field-level authority.

workflow-price|H|H5|authz|Checkout accepts the client-supplied price instead of calculating it from trusted product data. What is the primary flaw?|Trust in client-controlled business state|Missing DNS reverse lookup|An oversized cookie expiry|Use of a public-key certificate|The server should determine price and validate discounts using trusted rules. A signed-in user can still modify requests.|Business values require validation beyond type checking.

bulk-authorization|H|H5|authz|A bulk export checks ownership only for the first requested record. What must change?|Authorization for every included record|A higher maximum export size|One global check that the list is nonempty|Alphabetical sorting of record IDs|Batch operations must enforce the applicable permission on all objects, not one representative.|One authorized item does not authorize the batch.

deny-default|H|H5|authz|A new API route is accessible because no access policy matched it. Which design would prevent this default?|Deny unless access is explicitly allowed|Allow until a user reports misuse|Use obscure route names|Remove access logging|Deny-by-default reduces accidental exposure when routes or resources are added.|Missing policy should not mean unlimited access.

horizontal-vertical|H|H5|authz|Two ordinary users can read each other's notes, without gaining administrator privileges. What kind of escalation is demonstrated?|Horizontal access-control failure|Vertical role escalation only|Cryptographic key substitution|Network route poisoning|The requester crosses peer-user boundaries. Vertical escalation instead crosses privilege levels.|Describe the actual authority boundary crossed.

type-range|H|H6|rest|A transfer amount is numeric but accepts negative values, reversing the debit. Which validation is missing?|Business range constraints|HTML tag escaping|Public key pinning|Cookie domain narrowing|Valid syntax is only the first step. Enforce domain rules such as positive amounts and limits.|A well-typed value can still be invalid business input.

server-validation|H|H6|rest|A browser rejects invalid quantities, but the API accepts the same quantities directly. Where should the rule be enforced?|On the server handling the operation|Only in the HTML maxlength attribute|Only in CSS for the quantity field|Only in the user's local storage|Client validation improves feedback; server validation enforces the rule against modified clients.|The requester controls the client.

canonical-order|H|H6|rest|A security check sees one URL-decoding pass, while the file handler decodes again. What risk does this create?|Validation and use can see different paths|Every URL becomes a database query|TLS negotiation becomes case-sensitive|The server cannot log query strings|Normalize consistently and validate the representation actually used. Extra decoding may reveal syntax after a check.|Validation must match the consuming parser.

allowlist-identifier|H|H6|sqli|A sort column cannot be represented as a SQL value parameter. What is a suitable design?|Map permitted names to fixed identifiers|Concatenate any submitted identifier|Escape only spaces in the column name|Treat the column name as a password|Identifiers and values have different roles. Select fixed known columns through an allowlist mapping.|Value parameterization does not parameterize query structure.

length-budget|H|H6|rest|An API accepts arbitrarily large arrays of otherwise valid items. Which rule helps limit resource exhaustion?|Collection-size and processing limits|HTML encoding of every integer|A default green button|A longer session cookie path|Validate size as well as individual items and apply appropriate resource limits.|Valid elements can form an excessive request.

ldap-filter|H|H10|ldap|Input is joined into an LDAP search filter. Which escaping context applies?|LDAP filter escaping|LDAP distinguished-name escaping only|HTML text escaping only|SQL string escaping only|LDAP filter syntax and DN syntax have different escaping rules. Use a safe API or the correct context-specific treatment.|The destination grammar determines the defense.

ldap-dn|H|H10|ldap|A user-controlled value is inserted into an LDAP distinguished name. Which defense matches this sink?|DN-specific escaping and validation|SQL parameter binding alone|JavaScript string escaping alone|Replacing only HTML angle brackets|Distinguished-name values have grammar rules separate from LDAP filters. Handle them with the corresponding safe mechanism.|One LDAP escaping routine is not automatically suitable everywhere.

command-argv|H|H10|command|A process API passes arguments directly without a shell. Why can untrusted input still be dangerous?|It may supply harmful options to the program|It must always be parsed as shell syntax|It automatically receives filesystem isolation|It can no longer contain spaces|Removing the shell reduces shell injection, but argument injection remains possible. Validate allowable values and option handling.|No shell does not mean no dangerous interpretation.

shell-string|H|H10|command|A server concatenates a filename into sh -c command text. Which redesign most directly removes shell interpretation?|Use a direct API with validated arguments|Base64-encode the full command then decode it in sh|Add a hidden input to the form|Rely on the browser's filename picker|Avoid shell command construction where possible; safe argument boundaries still require validation.|Encoding transported text does not change the final parser.

xxe-parser|H|H10|xxe|An XML parser resolves attacker-specified external entities. Which behavior is relevant?|Reading local resources or making server requests|Changing every XML tag to uppercase|Verifying the user's password hash|Granting database administrator roles|Entity resolution can cause file disclosure or server-side requests depending on parser capability and environment.|XML well-formedness does not establish safe entity handling.

xxe-defaults|H|H10|xxe|An application changes XML libraries after disabling entities in the old parser. What must be verified?|The new parser's effective entity and DTD settings|Only that responses still contain XML tags|Only that the package has a shorter name|Only that the browser supports XML|Security defaults differ by parser and version. Recheck the effective configuration and behavior.|A control belongs to the actual parsing path.

eval-input|H|H10|rest|A calculator implements user expressions with a general-purpose eval API. What is the main design concern?|Untrusted data is interpreted as program code|All arithmetic is necessarily inaccurate|Every request becomes a TLS handshake|HTML forms cannot send numbers|Use a constrained expression parser or permitted operations rather than general execution of untrusted code.|Feature requirements rarely justify a complete language interpreter.

upload-extension|H|H6|upload|An upload trusts a filename ending in .jpg without inspecting content. Which assumption is unsafe?|The extension proves file type|The server can store more than one file|The filename may contain a dot|The uploader can choose an image size|Use layered checks, safe storage, size limits, and appropriate content validation; extensions are client-controlled.|A label does not establish content or safe processing.

upload-storage|H|H6|upload|Why store uploads outside a directory where the web server executes scripts?|To separate uploaded data from executable content|To make filenames cryptographic keys|To disable all application authentication|To guarantee uploads contain no malware|Non-executable storage limits one route to code execution. Other upload and processing controls remain necessary.|Storage placement mitigates a specific consequence.

upload-contenttype|H|H6|upload|The request declares Content-Type: image/png. What does that establish by itself?|The client's claimed media type|A verified PNG file signature|A clean malware scan result|A safe image-decoder configuration|The request header can be forged. Independently validate content and handle files defensively.|Client metadata is evidence of a claim, not verification.

traversal-root|H|H6|upload|A file-download API joins a supplied relative path to a storage directory. What invariant should it enforce?|The resolved target remains inside the permitted root|The supplied string has at least five characters|The URL contains a filename extension|The path is displayed in a disabled textbox|Resolve and validate paths with appropriate platform rules and consider symlinks. A prefix or substring check alone can be misleading.|Validate the actual resource selected.

ssrf-redirect|H|H6|ssrf|A URL fetcher validates the initial destination but follows redirects without checks. What can happen?|A permitted URL redirects to a forbidden destination|Every HTTP response becomes a password reset|The browser gains server filesystem permissions|Redirects disable network routing|Apply destination restrictions to subsequent requests as well as the initial URL.|The final destination can differ from the submitted one.

ssrf-dns|H|H6|ssrf|A hostname passes an IP check, then resolves differently when fetched. Which issue needs handling?|DNS resolution and connection consistency|HTML attribute quoting|Password-reset expiry|Database transaction isolation|A validation-to-use gap can undermine destination restrictions. Validate actual connection destinations and use appropriate network controls.|A hostname is not a fixed IP address.

ssrf-schemes|H|H6|ssrf|An intended HTTP fetcher also accepts file: and other URL schemes. Which restriction is appropriate?|Allow only required schemes and destinations|Permit any scheme with a short name|Reject only URLs containing spaces|Check only that the URL has a colon|Restrict the capabilities exposed by the fetcher. Different handlers may access local or unrelated resources.|A syntactically valid URL need not be an allowed operation.

errors-trace|H|H8|err|A malformed request exposes a stack trace with source paths and SQL text. What should the public response provide?|A generic error with an internal correlation ID|The full traceback plus the database password|Every environment variable for diagnosis|A promise that all errors are harmless|Keep useful diagnostic detail in controlled logs, and expose a limited message and correlation identifier to the client.|Debugging value does not require public internals.

debug-production|H|H8|err|A production exception page offers an interactive debug console. What is the priority?|Disable public debug functionality|Rename the page's CSS classes|Add a longer description of the exception|Hide only the browser address bar|Interactive debugging can expose powerful execution or inspection features. Production access needs appropriate restrictions.|A development convenience can become a production capability.

log-secrets|H|H8|session|An error handler logs full Authorization headers. What improvement is needed?|Redact credentials while retaining diagnostic context|Increase only the log font size|Publish logs to improve transparency|Hash only the HTTP status code|Logs should support investigation without duplicating bearer secrets. Apply access control and retention rules too.|Observability should not create another credential store.

xss-text|H|H9|xss|Untrusted text is assigned to textContent rather than innerHTML. Why does this help?|It treats the value as text rather than markup|It cryptographically signs the DOM|It removes every possible script in the page|It changes the site's origin|Using safe text sinks avoids HTML interpretation in that operation. Other sinks still need review.|Safe handling is specific to the destination.

xss-context|H|H9|xss|HTML text encoding is reused for input inserted inside JavaScript source. What is wrong with this approach?|The output contexts have different grammars|JavaScript cannot contain user data|HTML encoding always signs scripts|All encoded characters are removed by TLS|Use context-appropriate handling or avoid dynamic executable contexts. HTML encoding is not a universal injection defense.|Ask which parser consumes the output next.

xss-stored-location|H|H9|xss|A malicious profile biography executes only when a moderator views it later. Which classification fits?|Stored XSS|Reflected XSS only|Blind SQL injection only|Session fixation only|The input is persisted and later reaches a browser execution context. Its delay does not make it safe.|The victim may be a different user on a different page.

xss-dom|H|H9|xss|A fragment identifier is copied into innerHTML entirely in browser JavaScript. What type of issue can result?|DOM-based XSS|A server-side SQL syntax error|An SMTP relay configuration flaw|A DNS zone transfer|The vulnerable source-to-sink flow exists in client code; fragment values normally are not sent in the HTTP request.|A server response review can miss client-side flows.

xss-httponly-limit|H|H9|xss|Session cookies are HttpOnly. Why can same-origin XSS still harm an authenticated user?|Scripts can perform actions using the browser session|HttpOnly makes every cookie publicly readable|The browser must disable all request headers|The attacker automatically knows the password|Cookie read protection does not stop malicious script from interacting with accessible application functions.|Protecting cookie values is only one layer.

csp-layer|H|H9|csp|A restrictive CSP is added while unsafe HTML insertion remains. What is the best security interpretation?|CSP adds defense in depth; fix the unsafe sink too|CSP makes all untrusted markup safe by definition|CSP replaces object authorization everywhere|CSP proves no browser can ever execute injected code|A policy can reduce exploitability but should not substitute for safe data handling and output controls.|Mitigations do not justify leaving the root cause.

url-javascript|H|H9|xss|Untrusted input becomes a link href after HTML encoding. Which additional check matters?|Allow permitted URL schemes|Pad the link text to a fixed width|Encrypt the HTML tag name|Convert the entire page to uppercase|HTML encoding addresses markup syntax, not dangerous URL semantics such as script-capable schemes.|A safely quoted attribute can still hold a dangerous value.

rich-text|H|H9|xss|A feature must retain some user-supplied HTML formatting. Which approach is suitable?|A maintained allowlist-based HTML sanitizer|Removing only literal script tags|Replacing only the first angle bracket|Trusting all HTML from signed-in users|A suitable sanitizer preserves permitted formatting while removing dangerous markup and attributes. Keep it updated and use it correctly.|Many executable constructs do not require a script tag.

tls-hostname|H|H12|tlscheat|A client accepts any trusted certificate without checking its hostname. Which attack remains possible?|Impersonation using a certificate for another name|Breaking AES by changing the URL path|Turning TLS into plaintext DNS|Changing every session cookie expiry|Chain trust and identity matching are separate checks. Validate the intended endpoint identity.|A trusted issuer did not certify every hostname for that certificate.

mixed-content|H|H12|tlscheat|An HTTPS page loads an active script over HTTP where the browser allows it. What is exposed?|Integrity of the page's active code|Only the spelling of the page title|The private key of every certificate authority|Only the server's local database backup format|A modified script can alter the protected page's behavior. Browser blocking behavior is part of the assessment, not an assumption to ignore.|Secure delivery of the main document does not cover insecure dependencies.

hsts-first|H|H12|tlscheat|Why can HSTS learned from a response leave a first-visit gap without preload or prior state?|The browser may not yet know the HTTPS-only policy|The policy encrypts only the second cookie|HSTS requires all URLs to contain a token|HTTPS cannot serve policy headers|An initial HTTP visit may precede learning the policy. Preload and previously learned state affect this scenario.|Distinguish existing browser state from a fresh client.

token-https|H|H12|tlscheat|An API uses bearer tokens but permits HTTP. What does token strength fail to protect?|Tokens exposed in transit|Only the token's JSON field order|The public server banner length|Only the account display name|A captured bearer token may be replayed. Use protected transport and avoid leaking tokens into other channels.|Unpredictability does not protect a token after disclosure.

cors-credentials|H|H5|cors|An API reflects arbitrary Origin values and allows credentialed reads. What should be reviewed?|Whether untrusted origins can read sensitive responses|Whether every response has a numeric status|Whether origins contain a dot|Whether the API uses POST anywhere|Credentialed CORS should allow only trusted origins where needed. Test browser-observable behavior and sensitive data access.|A syntactically valid origin need not be trusted.

cors-null|H|H5|cors|An API trusts Origin: null for credentialed sensitive responses. Why is this dangerous?|Multiple opaque-origin contexts can produce null|null names a single trusted corporate domain|null guarantees the requester is offline|null disables all browser credentials|Sandboxed and other opaque-origin contexts can serialize as null. It is not a unique identity for one trusted application.|Special origin strings still require a trust decision.

cors-authz|H|H5|cors|A native client ignores CORS restrictions and accesses a privileged API. Which control must protect the API?|Server-side authentication and authorization|Only the browser's origin-read policy|Only a frontend hidden button|Only the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header|CORS governs browser access to responses, not general server authorization for arbitrary clients.|A browser policy cannot secure every client type.

config-backup|H|H13|apache|A web directory exposes .bak files containing old source and secrets. What is the relevant correction?|Keep sensitive backups outside served paths|Rename .bak to another guessable suffix|Disable only POST requests|Remove links while serving files unchanged|Do not serve deployment artifacts and secrets as public content. Removing links is not access control.|Assess resources reachable without navigation links.

default-admin|H|H13|authn|A deployment exposes a default administrator account with vendor credentials. What should be done?|Replace default credentials and restrict management access|Change only the login page's logo|Keep the credentials if the hostname is obscure|Publish the password in a help tooltip|Known defaults are a common entry point. Control the account and the management surface according to deployment needs.|Obscurity does not change a known credential.

security-headers|H|H13|csp|A scanner reports one missing security header. What determines the finding's practical significance?|The header's relevant threat and actual application behavior|The fact that every absent header has critical severity|Only the number of HTTP response bytes|Only whether the site has a modern logo|Assess the protection intended, existing controls, and applicable behavior. A header checklist alone cannot establish impact.|Name the attack or consequence the missing control enables.
